front: Binoculars, spotting scope, rifle scope: the three jobs?
back: Binoculars find. Spotting scope judges. Rifle scope only aims (Tip). Never glass with the rifle scope: the muzzle follows your eye (95%).
42 ÷ 8 = 5.25 mm. Front lens ÷ power (85%, Vortex).

front: Your pupil at dawn or dusk?
back: About 4 to 5 mm; in bright light 2 to 3 mm (85%, Vortex). Big exit pupils matter most in the first and last light.
8x or 7x: Vortex calls them adequate for woodland; 10x for greater distances (85%).
A steady view shows the tiny ear flick or tail twitch a shaky view hides (65%, goHUNT).

front: How long does Josh Kirchner (onX) glass one spot?
back: About one hour at a time before moving (65%).

front: Glassing order: near first or far first?
back: Your call. Kirchner (onX): close and obvious first. Warren (Western Hunter): furthest points first, before heat haze (65%). Both: naked eye, quick pass, slow grid.
About a third of each binocular view (60%). Slow strips, then glass it all again.

front: Why glass far ground early in the day?
back: Heat waves (mirage) blur far slopes as the day warms (65%, Remi Warren).

front: Where should the sun be when you glass?
back: Behind you or to the side: the animal is lit, you are in shade (Tip).

front: Name four 'parts' to look for when glassing.
back: A flat horizontal back line, the ear V, vertical leg poles, a flicker of movement. Also a white rump, an antler glint (65%).

front: Found one in the binoculars. First move?
back: Do not move. Keep eyes on it, pick two landmarks, judge it with the scope (Tip).

front: Glassing from the truck with a rifle inside: legal?
back: Hunt includes searching with a firearm (page 3) and hunting from a motor vehicle is unlawful (item 22) (99%). How they apply here: ask a conservation officer (VERIFY).

front: Where do you measure a print in mud or snow?
back: The floor of the print, not the rim. Average 3 to 5 prints (80%).
Stride: same foot to the same foot (2 steps). Straddle: trail width, outside left to outside right (75%).
About 5.7 to 10 cm (80%, North Dakota Game and Fish). Moose 11.4 to 17.8 cm.

front: Faster gait does what to stride and straddle?
back: Longer stride, narrower straddle (85%).

front: Stot or gallop groups leaving a bed mean?
back: It was spooked, maybe by you. Walking tracks out: it left on its own (80%).

front: Tapered rope scat with hair: which family?
back: Dog family: coyote, wolf, fox (75%). Gloves and a stick: a tapeworm risk in parts of BC (85%).

front: Blunt segmented scat, sometimes scratched over?
back: Cat family: cougar, bobcat, lynx (75%).
An oval about 0.9 to 1.2 m long, flattened, with hair and pellets (70%).

front: How high are most deer rubs?
back: About 30 to 105 cm. Centred 75 cm or higher suggests a mature buck (60%). Height beats tree size.
About 1.2 to 1.5 m above the pawed soil (65%).
About 80% from mid October to mid November; most visits at night (65%).

front: Plucked whole quills on a stump: who?
back: Likely a bird of prey. Bitten, wet, clumped feathers: a mammal (60%).
About 20 cm. Quail bowls 7 to 15 cm (65%).
Sharp edges, moist, shiny. Old: rounded, dry, debris or web inside (65 to 70%).

front: Rain pits inside a print mean?
back: Made before the rain. Clean print on pitted ground: after (70%).
Made after the frost formed, often this morning (65%).
Flag the last sure print, circle 10 m then 20 m; never walk on the trail (Tip, 70%).

front: Following a track with your rifle is what, legally?
back: Hunting: following on the trail of wildlife with a firearm (95%). Hours and land rules apply.

front: Is the '297 million receptors' figure a measured fact?
back: No. An early 1990s estimate; experts think it may be low (65%, Outdoor Life 2026).

front: Steady wind cone versus light wind cone?
back: Steady: long and narrow. Light: short and wide. Swirl: everywhere, back out (Tip).
Soon after the sun strikes the slope; east faces first (75%, Fire Weather handbook).

front: Which slopes flip uphill first, strongest, last?
back: East first, south strongest near midday, west by mid afternoon (75%).
About 5 to 13 km/h (3 to 8 mph). Downslope at night 3 to 8 km/h (75%).

front: Lee side of a ridge crest?
back: Air can tumble back uphill (70%). Do not sit just behind the crest (Tip).
Upslope above the canopy, but a thin cool layer can still slide downhill on the floor (75%).

front: Forecast wind versus head height wind?
back: Forecast is for 10 m; at 2 m wind may be 50 to 70% of it (90%).
Puffer bottle, milkweed, lighter flame, thread on the sling (70%, Tip).

front: Wind wrong for seat A on the morning?
back: Go to seat B planned for that wind. Never force A (Tip).
No source here proves a product stops a deer smelling you (60%). Play the wind (Tip).
Still hunting: slow walking to find an animal. Stalking: closing on one you have seen (70%).
2 or 3 steps, then look 20 seconds or more; a few hundred metres an hour (Tip).
Weight back, outside edge of the ball down, roll in, heel, then shift weight (65%).
Wet moss and grass, soft new snow. Loudest: dry leaves, crust, gravel (Tip).
Low ground the animal cannot see into. Move fast there, slow in its sight (Tip).
Shape, shine, shadow, silhouette, spacing, movement (70%, military teaching).
Two cones, no red cone: blue stands out; orange, red, green look dull (75%, National Deer Association).

front: Deer stares at you mid step?
back: Freeze, even on one leg, until it feeds again. Hold longer than it does (Tip).
One moves, one watches and signals. Hand signals, not voices (Tip).
Between bed and feed, downwind of the trail, in before first light (Tip).

front: Most tree stand falls happen when?
back: Climbing up or down or getting in and out: about 60% (70%, Iowa DNR (Department of Natural Resources) with Tree Stand Safety Awareness).
Always inspect, Buckle on a full body harness, Connect before your feet leave the ground (70%).

front: How does the rifle get up the tree?
back: Unloaded, on a haul line, after you are clipped in (80%, Wisconsin DNR (Department of Natural Resources)).
Can occur in under 20 minutes and can be fatal (80%, Wisconsin DNR).

front: UW (University of Wisconsin) study: harness use among 117 injured stand hunters?
back: Only 4 reported any harness use; 55% of injuries involved the spine (75%).

front: Electronic calls are legal for which animals?
back: Wolf, coyote, cougar, lynx, bobcat and Schedule C birds only (99%, page 12 item 41).

front: Mouth grunt tube for deer: legal?
back: Yes: not recorded or electronic (95%, my reading).
Unlawful for game birds (99%, item 42). Fake decoys: allowed.

front: Coyote calling: wind in your face or crosswind?
back: Your call. Wilson (Outdoor Canada) prefers downwind; Nemnich and Wood prefer crosswind (65%). All: watch the downwind side.
About 20 to 50 yd in front or upwind (60 to 65%, several callers).
Laser rangefinder, scope reticle, eye methods; laser first (70%).
Metres = size in metres × 1,000 ÷ mils (85%, Vortex).
Bright light, sun behind you, snow or water, clear air, a hidden dip (80%, Canadian Army).

front: Your .308 drop, 100 m zero, at 200 / 250 / 300 m?
back: About 13, 28 and 48 cm low with 150 gr (75%).

front: 20 km/h crosswind drift at 250 m (150 gr .308)?
back: About 27 cm, more than the vitals (75%).
About 70% of the full value (85%).

front: Steep shot: which distance to hold for?
back: The flat distance: slope × cosine. 30° makes 250 m into 217 m (95%).
Prone, sitting, kneeling, standing (85%, hunter education).
Shoots high. Pad under the forend (85%, hunter education).
Where the rifle points with muscles relaxed; move your body, not the rifle (80%).
Deep breath, let about half out, hold, slow press (85%).
Same positions and trigger, a fraction of the cost (65%); it teaches wind cheaply.

front: Rifle aim point on a broadside deer?
back: Up the back of the near front leg, one third up the chest (85%).
About 20 to 25 cm (75%).
Wait for the turn: bone in the way (85%, Tip).
The hump makes you aim high. Aim lower than instinct (65%).
Halfway up, tight behind the shoulder once the near leg steps forward (85%).

front: Long duck shot limit with steel?
back: 35 m (38 yd) is a long shot (70%).
About 100 in a 76 cm (30 in) circle at your longest range (70%, Ducks Unlimited).
No backstop, not 100% sure, moving, too far, through brush, lying down (70 to 85%, Tip).
No bullet reliably goes through brush; a twig can throw the shot (70%, American Hunter).
Decide early, range landmarks, look at the spot not the antlers, breathe out; shaking hard means let it walk (60%, Tip).

front: Mule kick and hard low run after the shot?
back: Often heart or lungs (70%).
Often a gut hit: mark it and back out for hours (70%).

front: Wait: heart or lungs, out of sight?
back: About 30 minutes; sources agree (70%).
Hours, longer than for a lung hit. Hunter Ed blog 4 to 6; National Deer Association 2012 2 to 4, 2023 8 to 10 (70%). Your call.
The longest wait of any hit. Hunter Ed blog 6 to 8 h or overnight; National Deer Association 2012 4 to 6 h, 2023 10 to 12 h; Pennsylvania at least 8 h (70%). Your call.
Lungs (65 to 70%). Dark, no bubbles: liver. Green bits: gut.

front: Which way does a blood drop tail point?
back: The way the animal went (80% physics, Tip in the field).
Downhill, to water and thick cover, often on a trail (70%).
About 10 m apart, each searcher in sight of the next (70%).

front: Tracking with rifle and headlamp after hours?
back: No: that is hunting outside hours and with a light (95%, 85% my reading).
All reasonable effort to locate, dispatch, retrieve and count it (95%, page 12).

front: Before you handle a big game kill?
back: Cancel your own species licence immediately (99%).
Below 4°C as fast as you can (80%).
4 to 60°C; bacteria can double every 20 minutes (80%).
At least 71°C; freezing does not kill wild Trichinella in bear (95%, CFIA (Canadian Food Inspection Agency)).
Spoils regardless of temperature (80%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
Never: plastic holds heat in. Cloth game bags, hung apart (80%).
Neck, ribs, four quarters and loins (95%, page 3).
About 4 for a deer, 8 for a moose (80%).
About 48% of field dressed weight (70 to 80%).
Assume loaded, Control the muzzle, Trigger finger off, See it is unloaded (85%).
Point safe, Remove cartridges, Observe chamber, Verify feed path, Examine bore (85%).

front: Zone of fire for each of two hunters?
back: About 45 degrees straight ahead; the middle and behind are no shot (75%).
Press, pack, tourniquet (75%).
Your call: 5 to 8 cm (American Red Cross, Stop the Bleed, 70%) or 5 to 10 cm (Canadian Red Cross 2012, 75%). Heart side, never on a joint.
Sources differ: older 2012 Canadian sheet says slowly release if bleeding dropped; newer sources say never. Ask your instructor (VERIFY).
Stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles (75%). Shivering that stops is an emergency.
Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Doubt means stay (75%).
Anything in threes: whistle, mirror, horn, fires (75%).

front: First call when you need help?
back: 911 on any phone; any tower in range (75%). No signal: satellite SOS (65 to 85%).
